This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, can be used to investigate the properties of black holes through the analysis of their electromagnetic spectra. A detailed examination of an AGN spectrum involves examining the spectral features of the material surrounding the black hole at the inner edges of its accretion disk. These features include: the iron K$\alpha$ line, modified by extreme gravitational effects near a black hole; the ultraviolet (UV) disk emission line resulting from the rotation of the hot, rapidly spinning disk near the black hole; and the Balmer line series emitted by the ionized hydrogen in the disk. By analyzing these features, researchers can determine the mass and spin of the black hole. In this work, we investigate the parameters that influence the shape of these features to optimize estimates of black hole mass and spin from observations of AGNs in the future. Utilizing an existing model, we generate synthetic spectra for different combinations of black hole masses and spins. These spectra can be used to training a machine learning algorithm to efficiently filter through potential parameters. This approach paves the way for utilizing upcoming observations from wide-field surveys to investigate the relationships between AGNs and their host galaxies, as well as to track the evolution of black holes over cosmic time.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelium as part of interkinetic
nuclear migration (IKNM). This process is closely linked to key signaling pathways,
transcriptional activity, and the spindle orientation that drives cell division.
Despite its importance, the underlying mechanisms driving migration patterns and
associated nuclear movements remain unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we created
nuclear-IKNM, a specialized module within the spatial explicit agent-based model
(SEABAM) framework. This module focuses exclusively on movement within the upper
and lower regions of tissue without dividing cells. By utilizing the model, we
investigated various nuclear and spindle properties that contribute to a accurate
replication of migration behavior. Our results show that interchanging low and
high-mobility states within the upper and lower regions successfully replicates the
characteristic migration pattern. Furthermore, a simple difference in spindle
orientation at the upper and lower limits of the upper region can account for the
upper and lower phase differences observed in the neural tube. Our model offers a
robust platform for exploring the development of IKNM across different tissue types.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for system operators.  To enhance accuracy, a programmer manually verified the initially obtained text from the ID card.  Following this, ease of data entry was achieved by applying Natural Language Processing in Python.  When tested with 15 samples, the combination of OCR and NLP demonstrated a high level of precision equivalent to 93.33%.  Consequently, this approach is deemed effective for creating an automated ID verification system.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates fast and efficient models for time series predictions, particularly valuable for systems with significant dynamics. As we aim to improve this technique and reduce the amount of training data required, a behavior with inherent time dependence was used as an example, specifically the Riemann hypothesis. Utilizing a sophisticated variant of reservoir computing with a sophisticated covariance structure that takes into consideration the correlations between different time series predictions, our study demonstrates superior results when compared to the traditional approach. In particular, our findings indicate more precise predictions can be achieved with less extensive training datasets, potentially in the thousands rather than millions. By leveraging a sophisticated strategy of combining multiple candidates through weighted combinations, a simpler version of this variant can be easily implemented with minimal overhead.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2018) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through a super-spreader event continues to spread among others.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both retrieval and direct generation in a unified training process.
Experimental results show that FLAN and T0 models can achieve substantial gains through this unsupervised method, with up to 1.5-point improvements on benchmark suites like GLUE and MultiTask, particularly in tasks where models often struggle.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, finding that its homotopy type matches that of a boolean complex of all groups. This simplifies to a collection of spheres when considering groups defined by an underlying set regarding which the longest element is well-defined.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The study focused on 14 key elements with significant stellar absorption: Na, Mg, Si, S, Ca, Ti, Fe, Ni, Cr, Mn, Al, Cu, Zn, and Sr. The abundance patterns were correlated with 'prompt' and 'delayed' supernovae types using a two-time-scale model. The results revealed a distinct element formation behavior: elements like Mg, Si, Ni, Sr, and Sr were formed primarily through 'prompt' supernovae, while others like S, Ti, Cr, Mn, Zn, and Cu were formed through 'delayed' supernovae. The study revealed a gradient in elemental distribution across the Milky Way disk: a steeper gradient in 'prompt' elements and a flatter one in 'delayed' elements. The results also indicated an age-related variation in the Milky Way disk: a smaller change in the 'prompt' elements and a more significant one in 'delayed' elements. The analysis of random abundance fluctuations revealed similar patterns to gradients across space: a smaller fluctuation in 'prompt' elements and a more significant one in 'delayed' elements. The study is expected to provide valuable insights into the relationships between the stellar elemental abundance gradients and supernovae types when combined with gas absorption data.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during design and failure analysis. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the study develops a coupled mechanical and thermal model based on the theory of multiphysics. In this approach, the difficult-to-measure crystallinity fraction is operationally defined through its impact on thermal properties, specifically melting temperature and heat flow absorption capacity. Bayes' theorem enables efficient estimation of a probabilistic damage variable from thermal responses to impact tests. Findings show that regions of high strain history exhibit induced crystallization, resulting in induced damage and Altschuler-Freeman anomalies. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio of variations to the mean in the energy density of quantum fields across various spacetime settings. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The proportion of these fluctuations to the mean value determines the validity of specific probability distributions. Calculating the free energy density allows the derivation of these quantities in 2d Casimir space, 2d Einstein cylinder, 4d ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe, as well as in Einstein universes of other spatial dimensions. The investigation of these quantities across various spacetime settings will enable assessments of quantum matter field stability and shed light on the fundamental issue of coexistence between quantum fields and spacetime settings.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands in contrast to previously established datasets centered on categorization or cause-effect dynamics, by prioritizing the seamless application of knowledge across various contexts.  ATOMIC's data pairs, consisting of sequential actions (doings), emerges as a valuable subset when viewed through the descriptor-based lens, while its flexible nature surpasses alternatives such as Doings2Causes or Causes2Doings.  Our research team developed a model demonstrating our proposed framework's necessity for completing complex task sequences, establishing the ATOMIC dataset as an essential tool for evaluating AI systems' abilities to tackle intricate tasks devoid of categorical constraints.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational complexity increases significantly for large-scale investment portfolios due to the hindering effect of coherent risks. Although Markowitz's modern portfolio theory is commonly used, its classical algorithms' time complexity increases quadratically in response to this issue. In contrast, the pioneering LHSQ method achieved a time complexity proportional to the square root of parameters by exploiting less stringent sparse conditions with iterative solvers, but non-sparse covariance matrices necessitate an impractical degree of quantum data encoding. This obstacle is overcome in our approach, which combines a variety of optimizations including the HHL algorithm for instantaneous Hamiltonian simulation, qubit-register amortization, and careful analysis of the portfolio-shaping operation to achieve significant reductions in time and space complexities. As a result, we obtain an agnostic time complexity and space complexity for solving portfolio-optimization concerns under coherent-risk-hindering conditions.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to effectively utilize text data for transfer learning and distillation, we've identified two key challenges in developing a solution using a multimodal training approach. Our proposed framework, TexT2TexT, aims to overcome these obstacles and uses an attention-based encoder to map input text to a latent representation, followed by a decoder to generate the target representation. By creating a contrastive loss between matching pairs and an attention regularization loss, TexT2TexT ensures that ASR models can capture semantic relationships between source and target languages. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method is particularly effective when the available labeled data is scarce.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$ are independent and identically distributed without replacement, drawing from the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+1\}$, with each position having a probability of $1/(n+1)$. Notably, this finding does not depend on the random uniform measure's parameter. Consequently, our results provide the first statistical analysis of random uniform parking distributions. This study builds on previous work conducted by Bousquet-M\'elo, Cortier, and Schachter. Our research also identifies the random uniform measure's parking distribution intermediate steps, demonstrating that they constitute exchangeable sequences exchangeable in the sense of de Finetti. This discovery leads to the discovery of an exchangeable step distribution and its profound relation to the Beta binomial distribution.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from dose reduction. A viable solution lies in computed tomography (CT) scans being performed silently and rapidly using low-dose PET-CT devices with ultrashort exposure times, which could mitigate their limitations. Utilizing state-of-the-art 120-image per second PET-CT scan technology, researchers conducted state trials using fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) with dose-reduced PET scans, yielding acceptable results. The study found that very low-dose PET-CT scans are feasible, even for precise measurement of FDG uptake in tumors less than one centimeter in diameter. These findings support using high-speed PET-CT scan technology for sensitive populations with minimal radiation exposure and adequate image quality.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and using computer-generated statistics, the authors examine the link between CT and various types of computer-generated coherence tasks, including summarization, classification, and prediction. The analysis reveals that to accurately predict the coherence of a text, the system must consider the content of unrelated statements, effectively demonstrating that coherence identification is more complex than previously thought. Furthermore, considering the alignment between statements' underlying elements provides a better understanding of classification and prediction tasks, in contrast to the current prevailing view. This study's novel perspective and findings will be utilized in upcoming research projects.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their efficiency in using bandwidth. To facilitate future research, the researchers made the code and datasets used in this study publicly available via GitHub.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

Theories explaining highly stretched polymer brushes are well-established for flat surfaces, but curved substrates pose more complex scenarios. Although initial models were developed for spherical substrates, they ignore the region near the 'pole' where polymers experience significant stretching discrepancies. This research derives a new end exclusion zone, specific to general curved substrates, to refine the theoretical analysis. A new variable, incorporating the pole's characteristics and end exclusion zone, is created to solve governing equations. Solutions obtained demonstrate that a new parameter defining intermediate brush behavior is universally applicable. Further analysis of this variable reveals that end exclusion zones significantly influence the transition regions of moderately stretched polymer brushes. Additionally, examples of mild to severely curved substrates are presented to illustrate the model's relevance.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also require additional validation due to input data that includes noisy photons, not just image pixels. Consequently, this study offers both valuable insights and practical guidelines for applying fermi-friendly machine learning algorithms.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based framework and find that it can achieve a range of approximations, from 2 to $\frac{5+\sqrt{13}}{2}$, depending on the specific problem being solved. We also explore various frameworks combinatorial optimization can be represented within, including matroid, submodular, knapsack, and general combinatorial optimization. When using basic frameworks such as these, we can obtain combinatorial values approximating the maximum possible social welfare. Additionally, we develop a model incorporating future desires and demonstrate that even then, we can achieve a range of combinatorial social welfare approximations, from $\frac{9}{5}$ to $\frac{7}{5}$, when using the serial dictatorship mechanism.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal fewer than 100 documented binary asteroids within a system where 
90 percent of asteroids exceed 5 kilometers in size, discovering asteroids 
with wide binaries holds significant implications for comprehending binary 
stability and calculating asteroid masses. Our innovative approaches were 
developed utilizing images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, incorporating 
subminute exposure depths reaching 22.2 magnitude over spatial spans 
of 400 megapixels. As these images frequently contain multiple asteroid 
components, we devised specialized models to reconstruct their evolving 
morphological patterns. The first proposed method, utilized in section 
\ref{sec:fitting}, involves creating a set of basis vectors through 
principal component analysis (PCA) from residual images, and determining 
binary parameters via maximum likelihood estimation. In contrast, the 
approach presented in section \ref{sec:neural}, relies on a convolutional 
autoencoder (CAE) to generate a set of PSF vectors, and identifies binary 
parameters that maximize the likelihood of observed images. In section
