This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be used to accomplish simple tasks without requiring a pre-existing language model for the system. To assess this, we examine if a role-playing game system can follow instructions given by a Dungeon Master, whose role is equivalent to providing the system with a teacher or critic signal. Our system consists of a large language model that can be guided by the Dungeon Master through examples, feedback, and corrections. We test this in a simplified version of Dungeons and Dragons, involving a graphical world with a defined set of objects and actions. Our challenge includes a multi-stage process: a Dungeon Master-defining stage, a gameplay stage, and an evaluation stage. In an contested contest using a warrior character in a battlefield setting, our system demonstrates a significant improvement over baseline methods, particularly when the Dungeon Master feedback is limited.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the mass gap. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the context of NG boson generation and the mass gap formation. A NG mechanism analogous to the Schwinger model has been presented through this bosonic kaon condensation model. Finally, potential applications of the anomalous NG theorem have been discussed across cosmology, high-energy physics, and dark energy research.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple conditions is often impractical or impossible due to its size and complexity.  In this work, we investigate the possibility of generating reliable outputs with a UNET-based model using only single-condition training data.  Our proposed method, known as the Biomedical Conditional GAN, utilizes the power of discriminators to learn the relationship between single and multi-condition data distributions without manually creating multi-condition labels.  Experimental results show that our model successfully generates images accurate both visually and functionally according to the desired condition.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, contradicting observations.  Moreover, some galaxies emitting high energy radiation cannot be explained by this model due to constraints from high energy X-rays and radio waves.  Alternatively, we proposed that magnetic fields formed during the "BJ" process could provide a unifying explanation for gamma-rays in these galaxies, if electrons in "landau" states annihilate by colliding with the gamma-rays and producing observable signals in the energy X-ray range.  In summary, the "MAD" model requires precise conditions to meet all constraints from gamma-rays, X-rays, and radio waves, and a common mechanism is needed to explain the gamma-rays in these galaxies.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data on the [II] emission lines at 102.7 and 8544 Angstroms are available, both locally and at various distances. Due to low excitation in molecular gas, the 102.7 Angstrom line often appears absent, which we used to estimate gas temperatures through a new, non-LTE-based excitation model. This in turn enabled us to determine gas densities and create a non-LTE correction factor for observing [II] emission. We found that most galaxies have gas temperatures between 3000 and 6000 Kelvinnn, with bulge disks exhibiting higher values than spiral structures. These differences in temperature have implications for estimating molecular gas from [II] emission in different galaxy types.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To achieve this, we created a Cayley graph that accurately represents all permutations
with a distance of up to r from a specified starting point.
As a direct consequence of this, we are able to determine the maximum possible
overlap between two metric spaces with a distance of r, where these spaces are at
least d units apart.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that in the case of bound states with spin-1, these conditions persist indefinitely, whereas they oscillate between atom and molecule forms in systems with spin-1/2. For collisions resulting in photon emission, we have also examined their impact, in the Born approximation, and discovered that while they lead to persistent atom-molecule conversion in both spin cases, they result in persistent atom-molecule pairs only in the spin-1 system, allowing for a stable Bose-Einstein condensate of bound states. External field effects, such as electric and magnetic fields, as well as electric and magnetic dipole fields, were also analyzed, as they may have a significant influence on the stability of these atom-molecule systems.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations provide an appropriate framework for modeling river flows, the task of predicting time-dependent flow velocities with a reliable numerical solver can be computationally demanding, especially for multiple prediction instances. In this study, several machine learning predictors are tested to replace the traditional solver and explore techniques for enhancing accuracy while maintaining efficiency. By examining different algorithms and combinations, we evaluate their performance in terms of precision and efficiency in relation to the original solver. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of lower-resolution solution inputs on predictive accuracy, discovering surprising results that reveal the complex relationships between machine learning training data and prediction outcomes.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of tasks within the domain. A key challenge lies in systematically categorizing the many concepts, methods, and theories under causal deep learning. We address this challenge by developing a comprehensive and adaptable conceptual framework that lays the groundwork for future research and review papers. Building upon this framework, we systematically examine various aspects of causal deep learning, including causal learning theories, methods, and applications across machine learning tasks. By highlighting the current status, limitations, and potential directions under each subdivision, we encourage further exploration within the field. Given the systematic nature of our proposed framework, it will also serve as a guiding structure for evaluating subsequent publications, potentially driving subsequent developments under each new and flexible subdivision.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model requires significantly fewer training data points when compared to another deep learning method previously used for high-resolution velocity reconstruction.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods designed to accommodate evolving tasks, including content-based query adaptation techniques. Building on this trend, we introduce a content-driven query adaptation framework for continual learning, called REPLAY, which employs a closed-loop system to automatically refine query attention in the exploration-driven reinforcement learning framework. Specifically, REPLAY utilizes a self-built knowledge graph, constructed from video content, to identify relevant learning episodes from past data based on the current test subject's profile. In order to tailor query attention to relevant historical episodes, we develop two value network modules that leverage graph-based representation to capture complex relationships within the test subject's implicit query. Value network modules include a GAT-based representation to capture non-linear interactions between confusion entities, and a Transformer-based representation to model long-term dependencies among multiple ambiguous terms. Our approach is evaluated using three meticulously constructed video retrieval datasets, including large-scale multimedia learning tasks from TV shows, and achieves record-breaking performance, surpassing the state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin, including the recently released techniques.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the suppression of disk star formation remains relevant as many massive star-forming galaxies are disappearing and observations indicate a relationship between the bulge to disk ratio and star formation rates. To investigate this correlation, our study utilized the SPARC database, compiling 390 galaxies' bulge and disk components from surface brightness profiles, along with associated data on their specific star formation rates, mass-to-light ratios, and local circular velocities. We developed empirical correlations between star formation and galaxy bulge properties, discovering that low S0 bulge values allow for normal star formation rates, whereas high S0 values restrict star formation to short spiral arms, akin to lenticular galaxies with stellar bars. Furthermore, we found distinct specific star formation rate correlations within bulges and disks, with bulges exhibiting a different specific star formation rate to light ratio correlation than disks and a steeper specific star formation rate to velocity relationship. Our research also revealed that galaxy mass to light ratios impact the specific star formation rate correlation, affecting both disks and bulges. Ultimately, our results provide a comprehensive understanding of how galaxy mass affects star formation rates in different components and can aid in interpreting observations of evolving star-forming galaxies.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and point-click neural interface elements. To support future research, the proposed method's code and the newly created features associated with the CEMR dataset are made available to the scientific community.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data that reveal the characteristics of their star-forming regions. These regions appear as compact, actively star-forming components situated at the outer edges of poorly defined, gas-rich, lopsided, and star-suppressed disks. We propose that the unique combination of features - specifically the suppressed star formation in the massive galaxy's disk - along with the presence of cosmic methanol emissions, results from a dynamic balance between magnetic fields sheared by differential rotation and gas currents generated by turbulent convection.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of enhanced angular momentum reacquisition through the transfer of angular momentum from the core to the outer layers, rather than angular momentum loss. This study paves the way for incorporating KIC 9267654's internal rotation characteristics into stellar evolution models, with the aim of better understanding the various internal rotation-inducing processes these stars undergo.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one with a new dataset, a process which is both time-consuming and expensive. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called FEN is introduced, capable of detecting false information on previously unseen events. The system achieves this by training an initial set of components, including sentence, document, and topic encoders, as well as a fake news classifier, which can be deployed across various languages and is resistant to distribution shifts, thereby facilitating the construction of the required label data using weak supervision, and ultimately, an ensemble-based classifier is utilized to detect false information. Additionally, the paper presents an incremental learning-based approach to build the necessary positive and pseudo-positive samples, allowing for precise labeling of previously unseen data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of FEN in identifying false information on previously unseen events.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, we investigate the influence of crystal orientation on the variance of dopant position required to produce a standard deviation in position variance that is comparable to the Coulomb interaction, finding that this variance is five times greater in silicon with a [100] orientation in comparison to silicon with a [111] orientation.
Quantum tunneling's behavior is inherent to the atomic configuration of defects in solids, which implies that quantum q-bits based on solid-state defects in [100] oriented silicon may exhibit greater variability than those in [111] oriented silicon, regardless of overall impurity density.
This study's findings have significant implications for the feasibility of ultra-low-power quantum computing based on silicon with [100] orientation.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of medical images treated with LITT, which can be difficult to obtain. In response, I presented a method called Constrained Thermal Response Mapping, which incorporates physical laws describing how heat spreads during LITT to augment the defined treated region, offering a novel way to artificially expand training data for deep learning models. Furthermore, I showed how this method can be applied to train a generative adversarial network to realistically simulate LITT-treated images, thereby increasing the available data for model training. Ultimately, these innovations can significantly enhance the precision required to evaluate the long-term results of LITT therapy.

GP 2, a graph-based language for efficient program analysis and verification, can be enhanced by implementing rooted rules in its graph transformation framework, reducing the computational complexity of certain verification tasks. Initially, the GP 2 interpreter lacked support for rooted rules and had difficulty handling programs with high data structures. By developing a GP 2 interpreter with rooted rules, known as GP 2rr, the team overcame these limitations, resulting in a speed boost of up to 10 times for certain verification tasks on complex programs. The GP 2rr interpreter's capabilities can be applied to a wide range of tasks, including checking program safety, finding bugs, and discovering features in complex data structures like Red-Black Trees, Lists, and Sets.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on various language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in multiple evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly enhances performance when applied to smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for managing large-scale knowledge graphs.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a dual-path convolution neural network based RNN model is here presented and evaluated. This model incorporates fast component convolution neural networks and a slow component RNN to capture temporal dependencies at both short and long ranges. Notably, a lookup table was added to the model to compensate for phase distortion introduced by the time-domain smoothing technique. Experimental results on the DNS challenge dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this model and provide a RNN framework that integrates dual-path architecture, yielding a 0.76 dB reduction in weighted signal-to-distortion ratio compared to the dual-path RNN baseline.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple yet effective single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the aim of representing atmospheric convection. This model includes closures for turbulent kinetic energy and heat/tensor turbulence fluctuations, allowing calculation of surface fluxes and subgrid-scale tendencies for thermodynamic and dynamic variables. A range of idealized test cases have been used to assess this model's performance, yielding successful results in handling cloud tests with varying stability and large-scale flow variations. The model also produces accurate phase-aggregated results that align with observed characteristics of real-world tropical convection systems. Furthermore, it accurately replicates the characteristics of convection observed in atmospheric models, resulting in realistic tropical precipitation patterns and long-term climate simulation.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups based on single-photon excitation.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of co-existing phases in the old and extended phase space settings, and also explore the thermal field in the presence of Yang-Mills fields.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a users field of view.
To accomplish this, a users head orientation must be determined, and existing
 solutions typically use vision-based methods. Although effective, these
 approaches depend heavily on visibility and fail in situations where key
 features are not discernible. To address this limitation, we present a novel
 approach based on prior knowledge. Our method uses a pre-trained
 classification model to identify the region a user is most likely to focus on,
 and then leverages this information, along with their previous head orientation
 history, to predict their current head orientation. We evaluate our approach
 on a dataset of real world interactions in a virtual tourism experience, and
 our results show that our method is capable of accurately determining the
 region of interest, and successfully predicting the users head orientation
 with substantial improvement over baseline methods. Ultimately, our work
 highlights the potential of prior knowledge-based methods to enhance users
 experience in virtual tourism by enabling more targeted and personalized
 streaming of 360-degree videos.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different
physical quantities within nonequilibrium quantum many-body systems. Such
models based on time evolution operators represented as tensors have formerly
yielded valuable results when applied to systems out of equilibrium, including
those described by the Ginzburg-Landau action with a specific set of symmetries.
However, until now it has not been possible to visualize the temporal dynamics
of systems with quantum many-body properties using the same type of approach.
Such properties are extensively manifested in the Faraday effect in a many-body
system of the Bloch-Berry model. This effect arises as a consequence of the
topological nature of nonequilibrium dynamics and manifests themselves in the
interplay of polarization currents resulting from an abrupt change in the
magnetic field. Due to their inherent nonstationary nature these currents will
continuously interact over time producing both individual and collective
nonperturbative responses, including a sequence of spectral peaks with both
equilibrium and non-equilibrium origins. Such findings may have significant
implications in distinguishing between perturbative and nonperturbative
quantum many-body effects in future experiments involving the measurement of
polarization currents via the associated electromagnetic fields.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary functionality and maintaining the unique magnetic properties. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating minute amounts of ferrimagnetic alloys within a gold nanoarray to create a highly complex crystal that reacts differently to light and controlled magnetic fields, resulting in clear and adjustable features in the spectral patterns. This discovery enables the development of precise light-sensing tools and provides a foundation for innovative technology that could manipulate magnetic properties with light in rare earth and transition metal alloys.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When trained data is available, this approach can be combined with white-box methods to enhance the efficiency of model compression. Conversely, when data is limited, it acts as a style transfer technique for neural networks, focusing on matching training data features rather than functional equivalence. Numerical experiments using real-world datasets and networks demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of this proposed approach.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with this approach is the reward signal sparsity problem, which hampers its practical application in real-world settings. Our solution involves shrinking the vocabulary network size to vestigial levels, which research indicates leads reinforcement learning to re-refine a neural translation's language structure. Furthermore, combining this technique with a note-based network reduction enhances effectiveness even more. Our findings show that this strategy boosts performance using adequate vocabulary and can increase efficiency while maintaining high speed and low reward sparse problem potential. Vestigial vocabulary network reduction is also applicable to other reinforcement learning optimization methods, including policy gradient and proximal policy optimization.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
We observe that the periodic driving force results in a constant average current,
indicating a non-equilibrium steady state. As the driving force becomes more intense,
we find that the system's non-equilibrium characteristics are significantly enhanced.
Furthermore, we observe that the system's behavior can become chaotically random,
which is indicated by an emergent entropy rate.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. A significant finding by Cobham in 1973 established that each unique base r requires a distinct finite automaton to identify integer bases r.
